name: @string-utility-belt/mcp

tools.name: list_utilities
tools.description: Search the string-transformation utilities this server can run (248 total, across categories like Encoding, Hashing, Ciphers, Compression, Data Formats, Analysis, Generators and more). Returns {items: [{id, name, category, description}], total, categories}, best matches first. Use this first to find an id, then call describe_utility for its exact parameters before run_utility. `category` and `query` combine (a utility must match both); omit both to browse the whole catalog. A category that does not exist matches nothing rather than failing, so take one from `categories`. There is no paging: when `total` exceeds the items returned, raise `limit` or narrow the query. Reads the bundled catalog only: no network access and no rate limit.

category.description: Category to filter to (case-insensitive), e.g. "Encoding" or "Hashing".

query.description: Search words, matched case-insensitively against id, name, tags, aliases and description; every word must match somewhere, in any order (e.g. "encode url", "sha256", "uppercase").

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default 50, max 500).

tools.name: describe_utility
tools.description: Full documentation for one utility: its parameters (kind, default, options/bounds, description), the value types it accepts/produces, tags, aliases, worked examples (input, inputEncoding, params and expected output — byte outputs there use the app's display format, while run_utility returns bytes as base64), and which runtime capabilities it needs. Call this before run_utility to learn the exact parameter names and defaults; skip it for a utility you have already described. `id` must be an exact, case-sensitive utility id: names and aliases are not resolved, so look those up with list_utilities first. An unknown id returns isError ("unknown utility: <id>"). When `unavailable` is set, run_utility and run_pipeline refuse the utility.

id.description: Utility id, as returned by list_utilities (e.g. "base64_encode").

tools.name: run_utility
tools.description: Run a single utility on `input` and return {output, outputEncoding?}. For two or more transformations in a row, make one run_pipeline call instead of chaining run_utility calls; if you do not know the id yet, find it with list_utilities. Plain text output is returned as-is; a JSON-producing utility returns pretty-printed JSON text; a byte-producing utility (e.g. gzip_compress, get_bytes) returns base64 with `outputEncoding: "base64"`. `inputEncoding` controls how `input` itself is decoded first: "text" (default) uses it as-is, "base64" or "hex" decode it to raw bytes, "json" parses it. Params are validated against describe_utility's spec; invalid ones are rejected. Input is capped at 1,000,000 bytes, output text past 1,000,000 characters is cut off (flagged `truncated`, with `fullLength`), and the call is stopped after 20s. A failing utility returns isError with the error message. Utilities that run arbitrary user JavaScript (e.g. "custom_js") are refused, and the few that need a browser DOM parser (e.g. "xml_to_json", "html_table_to_csv") fail here.

input.description: The value to run the utility on.

inputEncoding.description: How to decode `input` before passing it to the utility. Default "text".

params.description: Utility parameters (see describe_utility for names/kinds); params left out use their declared default.

tools.name: run_pipeline
tools.description: Run several transformations on `input` in one call: an ordered list of steps (string-utility-belt v3 schema), each step's output feeding the next. Besides utility steps, a pipeline can hold branches (parallel forks merged back together), macros (named sub-pipelines) and "run on each" steps (a sub-pipeline run on every line, delimited piece, JSON array element or JSON object value). Prefer this to chaining run_utility calls; for a single transformation, run_utility is simpler. Returns {output, outputEncoding?, errors, timings, skipped, halted}: `errors` maps step id to its error message, `timings` maps step id to milliseconds. Provide exactly one of `steps` or `share` (a `#/p/<payload>` share link, a full URL containing one, or the bare payload). Untrusted step data is sanitized first, so malformed entries are dropped rather than rejected. Refused outright: pipelines with more than 100 steps (nested steps counted), unknown utility ids, enabled steps with invalid params, and any step that would run arbitrary user JavaScript (e.g. "custom_js") — LLM-driven code execution is out of scope. Input is capped at 1,000,000 bytes, output text past 1,000,000 characters is cut off (flagged `truncated`, with `fullLength`), and the call is stopped after 20s.

steps.description: Pipeline steps (v3 schema). Each entry is either a utility step {id, utilityId, params?, enabled?, condition?, onError?}, a fork {type:"branch", id, branches:[[...steps], [...steps]], merge:{mode:"concat"|"zip"|"json"|"pick", ...}}, a sub-pipeline {type:"macro", id, name, steps:[...steps]}, or a map {type:"each", id, split:{mode:"lines"|"json-array"|"json-values"} or {mode:"delimiter", separator}, steps:[...steps], skipEmpty?} that runs `steps` on every item and puts the results back in place (on an each step, `onError` also decides what a failed item becomes). `condition` gates a step on its input ({kind:"always"|"nonEmpty"|"regex"|"type", ...}); `onError` is "passthrough" (default: record the error, pass the input on), "stop" or "empty". Use [] for the identity pipeline; omit when using `share`.

share.description: A share link (or its bare payload) for a previously built pipeline; used instead of `steps`.

tools.name: detect_format
tools.description: Guess what `input` is — JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, HTML, CSV/TSV, base64/base32/hex, URL-encoding, JWT, UUID, data URI, gzip/zlib, email, URL, IP address, unix timestamp, Markdown, SQL, Morse code, ROT13, plain binary — and return {candidates: [{format, confidence, note}]}, best first, confidence 0-1. Use it when you are handed an opaque or unlabelled value and must pick a utility for it; skip it when the format is already known. It only identifies, never transforms: to decode, search list_utilities for the top format (base64 -> base64_decode, JWT -> jwt_decode) and run that with run_utility. Ambiguous input yields several candidates (all-digit text can be a timestamp, JSON and hex at once); treat anything below about 0.45 as a weak guess. Use inputEncoding "base64"/"hex" only to deliver binary data such as gzip bytes: it is decoded before detection, so a base64 string you want identified must stay "text" (the default). Empty input yields an empty list.

instructions: 248 string and data transformations (encode/decode, hash, encrypt, compress, convert between JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV and XML, change case, format, analyse), run on this machine with no network access. Find a utility with list_utilities, read its exact parameters with describe_utility, then run it with run_utility. Several transformations in a row go in one run_pipeline call instead of a run_utility call each. detect_format identifies an unknown input (base64, JWT, gzip, …) before you pick a utility.
